faq.a: Mycobacterium tuberculosis preferentially involves the apical lung zones where oxygen tension is highest, and delayed diagnosis is common.
faq.q: Why is TB the top cause of upper‑lobe cavitation in East Africa?

faq.a: Yes, many TB cavities shrink or resolve after 6 months, but some may persist as fibrotic scars.
faq.q: Can a cavity disappear completely with treatment?

faq.a: If the chest X‑ray is equivocal, you need to assess wall thickness, look for a fungal ball, or evaluate for malignancy.

exam: What is the most likely diagnosis in a HIV‑positive patient with chronic cough, weight loss and a right‑upper‑lobe cavity on X‑ray? — Pulmonary tuberculosis; explain why upper‑lobe location and HIV increase suspicion.

How would you differentiate a tuberculous cavity from a lung cancer cavity on imaging? — Compare wall thickness, margins, and presence of nodules; consider CT characteristics and clinical risk factors.

A patient with a known cavity presents with sudden massive haemoptysis. What is your immediate management? — Stabilise airway, give high‑flow oxygen, position bleeding side down, arrange urgent bronchoscopy or embolisation.
If sputum AFB smear is negative but suspicion remains high, what is your next step? — Obtain Xpert MTB/RIF or culture; consider bronchoscopy if resources allow.
Why is fluoroquinolone avoidance recommended in initial TB therapy unless resistance is proven? — Fluoroquinolones can mask TB symptoms and promote resistance, compromising later standard regimens.

List three non‑infectious conditions that can produce upper‑lobe cavitation and how you would rule them out. — Lung cancer (CT + biopsy), aspergilloma (CT showing mobile ball), septic emboli (multiple peripheral lesions, blood cultures).
What nutritional advice should you give a patient with TB‑related cavitation? — High‑protein diet, vitamin D supplementation, avoid alcohol and tobacco.
When is surgical resection considered for a persistent cavity? — Persistent, large cavity with recurrent haemoptysis or failure to sterilise after 6 months of therapy, after multidisciplinary review.
ai.title: Upper Lobe Cavitation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Upper lobe cavitation on chest imaging signals lung destruction, most often due to pulmonary tuberculosis in low‑resource settings. Recognise the clinical picture, use targeted investigations, and start empiric anti‑TB therapy while ruling out mimics.

b: Cavitation = air‑filled space >1 cm with a definable wall
Upper lobes = right > left due to higher ventilation and gravity
sections.p: A radiolucent area within the lung parenchyma of the upper lobes surrounded by a wall of fibrotic tissue, visible on chest X‑ray or CT.

t.b: Does the image show a cavity in an upper lobe? – Presence confirms cavitation; location guides differential (TB most common).
What is the wall thickness and surrounding parenchyma? – Thin wall (<4 mm) suggests post‑TB scar; thick wall (>15 mm) raises suspicion for malignancy or fungal infection.

b: Small cavity (<2 cm) – mild disease, often early TB
Medium (2–4 cm) – moderate, may need prolonged therapy
Large (>4 cm) or multiple – severe, higher risk of haemoptysis and treatment failure
sections.p: Severity is judged by cavity size, wall thickness, and extent of surrounding disease; no universal staging system, but clinicians use a pragmatic three‑tier model.

b: Pulmonary tuberculosis (HIV co‑infection increases risk)
Bacterial lung abscess (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobes)
Fungal infection (Histoplasma, Aspergillus – especially in immunocompromised)
Bronchogenic carcinoma (less common but important)
Septic emboli from infective endocarditis
sections.p: In East African and other low‑resource hospitals the hierarchy of causes is dominated by infections, especially tuberculosis, followed by other endemic conditions.

b: Productive cough with occasional haemoptysis
Progressive weight loss and anorexia
Night sweats and low‑grade fever
Dyspnoea if cavity co‑exists with extensive disease
sections.p: Patients usually have a chronic cough (>2 weeks), weight loss, night sweats, and may cough up blood. Fever may be low‑grade or absent.
Select tests that answer the key clinical questions: is TB present, are there alternative pathogens, and how extensive is lung damage?

t.b: Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? – Positive smear confirms TB; negative does not exclude it.
Does the patient have TB and rifampicin resistance? – Rapid detection guides therapy; if unavailable, rely on culture.
What organism is growing and its drug susceptibility? – Needed for drug‑resistant TB or non‑TB pathogens.
Is the patient immunocompromised? – HIV positivity raises TB risk and influences treatment duration.
Is there anaemia or leukocytosis? – Anaemia common in chronic TB; leukocytosis may suggest bacterial abscess.
Are kidneys and electrolytes stable for anti‑TB drugs? – Baseline needed before starting therapy.

t.a: Bronchoscopy with BAL (if cavity not accessible and diagnosis unclear)
t.b: Can we obtain a sample for culture or cytology? – Useful when sputum is negative and malignancy is a concern.

b: Massive haemoptysis (>200 mL/24 h) – risk of airway obstruction
Secondary pneumothorax – sudden chest pain and dyspnoea
Bronchiectasis progression – recurrent infections
Spread to pleura → empyema
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and demand urgent action.

b: Standard 6‑month anti‑TB regimen (2 months HRZE, 4 months HR) – chosen for proven efficacy; avoid fluoroquinolones unless resistance suspected.
If bacterial abscess suspected, give clindamycin or amoxicillin‑clavulanate – covers anaerobes; avoid monotherapy with beta‑lactams alone.
For fungal cavities, itraconazole or voriconazole after confirming species – avoid amphotericin B unless severe disseminated disease.
Supplemental nutrition and vitamin D – improves immune response.
Monitor for drug toxicity (hepatitis, visual changes) – stop offending drug if severe.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; supportive care addresses symptoms and prevents complications.

b: Clinic review at 2 weeks, 2 months, end of therapy – assess symptom resolution and weight gain.
Repeat chest X‑ray at 2 months and end of therapy – look for cavity reduction; persistent cavity >6 months may need further evaluation.
HIV counselling and antiretroviral therapy if positive – reduces TB recurrence.
Smoking cessation and avoidance of indoor biomass smoke – lowers reinfection risk.
sections.p: Regular review ensures treatment success and early detection of complications.

b: Lung cancer (especially squamous cell) – tends to have irregular thick walls and nodular margins.
Pulmonary aspergilloma (fungal ball) – mobile intracavitary mass on CT.
Septic emboli from right‑sided endocarditis – multiple peripheral cavities.
sections.p: Several conditions produce radiolucent upper‑lobe lesions that can mimic TB cavities.

b: Negative sputum AFB does not rule out TB – up to 30 % of smear‑negative pulmonary TB.
Chest X‑ray may miss small cavities – CT is more sensitive.
Elevated ESR is non‑specific – can be raised in infection, malignancy, or inflammation.
sections.p: Certain investigations may give false reassurance.
